name: Every Surface Bright
description: An early holographic art film by Meridian-born director Nneka Johansson-Obi that renders grief as architectural space — the viewer moves through a series of rooms that physically reconfigure around emotional memory, with the laws of perspective and scale shifting according to the emotional temperature of each scene. The film emerged from Johansson-Obi's documentation of her own mother's death and was shown in unlicensed gallery spaces before a small licensed distributor gave it a limited release. It runs fifty-two minutes and has no dialogue.
cultural_impact: Every Surface Bright established holographic film as a legitimate medium for personal and emotional expression rather than spectacle, and its spatial grammar influenced two decades of holographic art and commercial design.
story_hooks: The original holographic projection files contain embedded personal data from Johansson-Obi's mother's medical records — included accidentally or deliberately is a question the director won't answer.
The Vantablack subsidiary that reverse-engineered the spatial techniques used them in a product that caused viewer disorientation injuries — and the original film may be the key to understanding why.
A Tier 1 street artist has been recreating scenes from the film at full scale in abandoned buildings using salvaged projection equipment.
